concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Nasal walls, septum and apertures
concepts.summary: Each nasal cavity is a wedge-shaped airway with a broad floor and narrow roof. The median septum, hard palate and skull-base roof separate it from the opposite nasal cavity, oral cavity and cranial cavity; the posterior choanae open into the nasopharynx.
keyPoints: The septum is formed mainly by septal cartilage anteriorly, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid superiorly and the vomer posteroinferiorly. Do not confuse the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid with the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone on the lateral wall.
The hard-palate floor is formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae anteriorly and horizontal plates of the palatine bones posteriorly. It is simultaneously the roof of the oral cavity.
The roof includes anterior frontonasal structures, a central cribriform plate and posterior sphenoid. The orbit lies lateral to the nasal cavity; the thin ethmoidal region is an important interface.

Nares are anterior openings with flexible cartilage and soft-tissue margins. Choanae are rigid posterior openings bounded inferiorly by horizontal palatine bone, medially by vomer and laterally by medial pterygoid plate.
The choanal roof involves the ala of the vomer and vaginal process anteriorly and sphenoid body posteriorly. A posterior view therefore differs from an anterior nostril/speculum view.
The external nose combines nasal bones and frontal maxillary processes with septal and alar cartilages. The major alar cartilages contribute to the flexible margins of the nares.
A deviated septum can narrow an airway; a bulging septum on a speculum view is not itself a nasal concha. Use the floor, septum and lateral conchae together to orient the image.
examTraps: The vomer is part of the medial wall, not a nasal concha.
Nares and choanae are different openings; only the latter communicate directly with the nasopharynx.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Reconstruct the nasal cavity from its four walls and two openings.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Medial wall: septum; floor: hard palate; roof: frontonasal, ethmoidal and sphenoidal components; lateral wall: conchae and their bony supports. Nares open anteriorly to the exterior, whereas choanae open posteriorly to the nasopharynx.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What bones form the main rigid choanal margins?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Vomer medially, horizontal plate of the palatine bone inferiorly, medial pterygoid plate laterally, and sphenoidal/vomerine components at the roof.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Vestibular, respiratory and olfactory regions
concepts.summary: The nasal cavity is not lined uniformly. Its skin-lined vestibule filters large particles, its extensive respiratory region conditions and clears inspired air, and its small superior olfactory region contains the receptors for smell.
keyPoints: The vestibule is the dilated region immediately inside each naris. Skin and hair follicles distinguish it from the respiratory mucosa farther posteriorly.

The respiratory region forms most of the cavity and contains ciliated and mucus-producing cells over a rich vascular bed. Mucus captures particles; ciliary transport carries it posteriorly for swallowing.
The olfactory region occupies the apex of the cavity, including the superior septal and lateral-wall region. Its high position is distinct from the inferior-meatus tear-drainage route.
Conchae increase mucosal surface area and air–tissue contact. Their vascular submucosa helps alter the temperature and humidity of inspired air.
Olfactory axons cross the cribriform plate to reach the olfactory bulb. General nasal sensation instead uses trigeminal branches; a sensory complaint is not automatically an olfactory-nerve problem.

The lecture lists warming/moistening air, reduced skull weight and voice resonance among the functions associated with paranasal sinuses. These do not replace the more direct conditioning role of nasal respiratory mucosa.
examTraps: Olfactory epithelium is not the lining of the entire nasal cavity.
A hair-containing lining just inside a nostril is vestibular skin, not ordinary respiratory epithelium.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Compare the three nasal regions by location and function.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The vestibule lies inside the naris and filters with hairs; the large respiratory region conditions air and clears mucus; the superior olfactory region detects odorants.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why do conchae improve nasal air conditioning?
retrievalPrompts.answer: They increase mucosal surface area and contact with air, exposing it to a richly vascular, mucus-covered respiratory surface.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Conchae, meatuses and sinus drainage
concepts.summary: The conchae organize four named air channels and a reproducible drainage map. Most sinus openings cluster around the middle meatus, whereas posterior ethmoidal cells, the sphenoidal sinus and the nasolacrimal duct have different destinations.
keyPoints: Superior and middle conchae are parts of the ethmoid; the inferior concha is a separate bone. The meatus named for a concha lies immediately inferior to it.
The inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct. It is not the usual opening of a paranasal sinus.
The middle meatus receives frontal, maxillary and anterior/middle ethmoidal drainage. A swollen or obstructed middle-meatus region can therefore affect several neighboring sinus pathways.
The ethmoidal bulla is an elevation produced by middle ethmoidal cells, which open on it. The semilunar hiatus lies inferior to the bulla and is associated with the uncinate process.

The ethmoidal infundibulum communicates with the anterior end of the semilunar hiatus. In the book’s standard arrangement, the frontal sinus drains through the frontonasal duct into the infundibulum and then the middle meatus.
Anterior ethmoidal cells drain toward the infundibulum/semilunar-hiatus region; the maxillary opening lies in the semilunar hiatus. Middle ethmoidal openings are on the bulla.
Posterior ethmoidal cells open into the superior meatus. The sphenoidal sinus opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha.
The conchae can obscure openings in an intact lateral-wall view. Partly removed-concha diagrams expose the same routes, not a different set of sinuses.
examTraps: Superior meatus receives posterior ethmoidal cells, not the sphenoidal sinus.
Middle ethmoidal cells open on the bulla; the maxillary opening is associated with the semilunar hiatus.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Draw the drainage map without looking.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Inferior meatus: nasolacrimal duct. Middle meatus: frontal, maxillary, anterior and middle ethmoidal sinuses/cells. Superior meatus: posterior ethmoidal cells. Sphenoethmoidal recess: sphenoidal sinus.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Relate bulla, semilunar hiatus, uncinate process and infundibulum.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The bulla projects into the middle meatus above the semilunar hiatus. The uncinate process helps delimit the hiatus, whose anterior region communicates with the infundibulum and the frontal drainage pathway.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Frontal and ethmoidal sinuses: orbital and drainage relations
concepts.summary: Frontal sinuses and ethmoidal air cells lie close to the orbit but do not all share one drainage channel. The ethmoid is both a nasal-wall bone and a thin orbital boundary, so its air-cell arrangement matters more than memorizing a single undivided “ethmoid sinus.”
keyPoints: Frontal sinuses occupy the frontal bone and drain by the frontonasal duct toward the infundibulum and middle meatus. The illustrated sinuses vary in size and shape rather than forming obligatory mirror images.
Frontal sinus sensation is associated with supraorbital branches of V1; arterial supply includes anterior ethmoidal branches. Distinguish this from the V2 supply of the maxillary sinus.
Ethmoidal cells occupy the paired ethmoidal labyrinths. Their lateral boundary includes a thin orbital plate, making the orbit a close neighbor of the nasal ethmoidal region.
Anterior and middle ethmoidal cells drain to the middle meatus; posterior cells drain to the superior meatus. Middle cells create the bulla visible on a partly exposed lateral-wall diagram.

The ethmoid also provides the cribriform plate, perpendicular septal plate and superior/middle conchae. Different parts of one bone therefore participate in smell, the septum, orbital separation and airflow.

The developmental illustration shows small early cavities that enlarge with growth. Adult sinus size and pneumatization should not be assumed in a child; exact ages of radiologic appearance are not established by this set.
Coronal sections help distinguish medial ethmoidal cells between the nasal cavity and orbit from the larger maxillary cavities below the orbits.

Ethmoidal-cell sensation uses anterior/posterior ethmoidal branches of nasociliary V1 and V2 orbital branches through the pterygopalatine region; arterial supply uses anterior/posterior ethmoidal arteries.
examTraps: “Ethmoidal sinus” is a group of air cells with different drainage routes.
An orbital plate of ethmoid is not the same structure as its cribriform plate.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How can you recognize ethmoidal cells on a coronal nasal image?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Look medial to the orbit, lateral to the upper nasal cavity and superior to the maxillary sinus; they appear as multiple small spaces rather than one large inferior cavity.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is the middle meatus relevant to frontal drainage?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The standard frontonasal-duct route reaches the infundibulum and semilunar-hiatus region, which communicates with the middle meatus.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Maxillary and sphenoidal sinuses: clinically useful neighbors
concepts.summary: The maxillary sinus relates closely to the orbit and upper teeth, whereas the sphenoidal sinus lies beneath the central skull base. Their openings and neighboring structures explain quite different patterns of symptoms and anatomical access.
keyPoints: The maxillary sinus is approximately pyramidal: the nasal wall forms its base, its apex points laterally, its roof relates to the orbital floor, and its floor relates to the maxillary alveolar process.
Upper molar and premolar roots may be close to the maxillary floor. Dental and maxillary-sinus processes can therefore be anatomically related rather than completely separate problems.
The maxillary opening is relatively high on the medial wall and communicates with the semilunar hiatus in the middle meatus. It is not an opening in the lowest part of the sinus floor.
Infraorbital and superior alveolar branches of V2 supply sensation to the maxillary sinus; corresponding maxillary-artery branches supply it.
Sphenoidal sinuses lie in the body of the sphenoid and open into the sphenoethmoidal recess. Their position is posterior and superior to most of the nasal cavity.

The pituitary gland lies above the sphenoidal sinus; the optic apparatus and cavernous-sinus region are also close skull-base relations. The sinus is therefore an anatomical route toward the pituitary, not an extension of the maxillary sinus.
Sinus size and septation vary, and the local developmental slide shows growth from small early cavities. Do not infer a universal surgical geometry or age threshold from a schematic illustration.

Sphenoidal-sinus sensation is supplied by posterior ethmoidal V1 and V2 orbital branches through the pterygopalatine region; its arteries include pharyngeal branches from the maxillary system. This differs from the infraorbital/alveolar maxillary-sinus pattern.
examTraps: A maxillary sinus opening high on the medial wall does not imply gravity drains the whole sinus freely.
A transsphenoidal route relates to the pituitary, not the orbital floor.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Compare the important neighbors of the maxillary and sphenoidal sinuses.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Maxillary: orbit above and upper posterior teeth below. Sphenoidal: central skull base with pituitary above and nearby optic/cavernous-sinus structures.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace sensory supply to the maxillary sinus.
retrievalPrompts.answer: It is carried by maxillary-division trigeminal branches, particularly infraorbital and superior alveolar branches.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Nasal gateways and what passes through them
concepts.summary: Nasal nerves and vessels arrive by several distinct portals, not just the cribriform plate. Linking each opening to the space it connects prevents confusion between a nerve’s cranial origin and its final route into the nasal wall.
keyPoints: The sphenopalatine foramen connects the pterygopalatine fossa with the posterolateral nasal cavity, just superior to the posterior attachment of the middle concha.

The sphenopalatine artery, nasopalatine nerve and superior nasal branches of V2 pass through this foramen. The artery and nerve names do not indicate that they originate from the same parent structure.
The incisive canal connects the anterior nasal floor beside the septum with the incisive fossa in the oral roof. The nasopalatine nerve travels toward the palate through it.
The terminal greater palatine artery travels in the reverse direction: from the palate through the incisive canal into the nasal floor/septal region. Direction of travel is a useful discriminator.
Olfactory fibers use the cribriform perforations. The anterior ethmoidal neurovascular route reaches the anterior cranial floor and then the nasal cavity near this region.
Inferior nasal branches of the greater palatine nerve enter through small lateral-wall foramina. Infraorbital nasal branches and facial arterial branches can enter around the naris.
A patent foramen cecum can connect nasal veins with the superior sagittal sinus in some individuals; it is a variable route, not the obligatory route for every nasal vein.
examTraps: The incisive canal is not the sphenopalatine foramen.
V2 reaches the pterygopalatine fossa through foramen rotundum, but its nasal branches use more distal gateways.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: List the important contents of the sphenopalatine foramen.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Sphenopalatine artery, nasopalatine nerve and superior nasal branches of V2, passing between the pterygopalatine fossa and nasal cavity.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which two structures use the incisive canal in opposite directions?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Nasopalatine nerve travels from nasal cavity toward the oral roof; terminal greater palatine artery travels from the palate into the nasal cavity.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Nasal blood supply, epistaxis and venous connections
concepts.summary: The nasal cavity receives arteries from both external- and internal-carotid systems. Rich anastomoses condition air but also create common bleeding sites, while venous connections link the nose to facial, pterygoid and intracranial routes.
keyPoints: The sphenopalatine artery is the major nasal arterial supply and a terminal maxillary-artery branch. It enters through the sphenopalatine foramen and divides into lateral nasal and septal distributions.
The greater palatine artery also arises through the maxillary system but reaches the nasal floor from below through the incisive canal.
Superior labial and lateral nasal branches arise from the facial artery and supply anterior septal/vestibular regions. These are additional external-carotid routes.
Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries arise from the ophthalmic artery, an internal-carotid branch. Their contribution is why nasal supply cannot be described as entirely external carotid.

An anterior septal region contains clinically important arterial anastomoses and is a common source of epistaxis. The location is on the medial wall, not the lateral-wall middle-meatus drainage complex.
Venous channels follow routes toward the pterygoid plexus through the sphenopalatine region and toward facial veins anteriorly.

Ethmoidal/ophthalmic venous connections communicate toward the cavernous sinus. Some people also have a foramen-cecum connection toward the superior sagittal sinus; these are distinct intracranial routes.
Vascular filling changes the volume of the mucosal tissue around conchae and septum. A vascular mucosal swelling and a fixed bony obstruction are anatomically different.
examTraps: Ethmoidal arteries belong to the ophthalmic/internal-carotid route.
Anterior epistaxis and posterior sphenopalatine entry are different landmarks.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace three external-carotid routes and one internal-carotid route to nasal mucosa.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Maxillary→sphenopalatine, maxillary→greater palatine, and facial→superior labial/lateral nasal are external-carotid routes. Internal carotid→ophthalmic→ethmoidal arteries is the internal-carotid route.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which venous connection links the nasal ethmoidal region to the cavernous sinus?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Connections through ophthalmic veins; this differs from the variable foramen-cecum route toward the superior sagittal sinus.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Nasal sensation, autonomic pathways and lymphatics
concepts.summary: Nasal innervation separates smell, general sensation and glandular autonomic control. General sensory branches may carry autonomic fibers as passengers, so identifying V2 at the destination does not mean that the secretomotor fibers originated in the trigeminal nerve.
keyPoints: CN I carries olfaction. General sensation is principally V1 in the anterior region and V2 posteriorly, with regional overlap rather than an absolute straight-line boundary.
The anterior ethmoidal nerve is a V1 branch associated with the anterior nasal region. The nasopalatine nerve is a V2 route across the septum and toward the incisive canal.
Posterior superior lateral nasal branches and inferior nasal branches through the greater palatine pathway supply parts of the lateral wall.

Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers originate through CN VII and travel in the greater petrosal nerve. They synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion before postganglionic fibers accompany V2 branches to glands.

Sympathetic fibers are ultimately associated with upper thoracic outflow and synapse in the superior cervical ganglion. Postganglionic fibers reach the region through the carotid/deep-petrosal pathway or along vessels; the pterygopalatine ganglion is not their synaptic relay.
The greater and deep petrosal contributions meet in the nerve of the pterygoid canal. Sharing a carrier does not make their pre/postganglionic status identical.
Anterior nasal lymph can pass onto the face toward submandibular nodes. Posterior nasal and sinus lymph passes toward upper deep cervical nodes, sometimes through retropharyngeal nodes first.
The lecture gives additional nodal-level labels, but the core book route is retained here. Do not use this simplified regional map as a complete oncologic nodal-level atlas.

Despite its name, the posterior ethmoidal nerve normally ends in ethmoidal-cell and sphenoidal-sinus mucosa rather than continuing into the nasal cavity itself; the anterior ethmoidal nerve has the prominent intranasal course.
examTraps: The pterygopalatine ganglion relays parasympathetic fibers, not the general sensory V2 axons.
Posterior nasal lymph and lower anterior nasal lymph do not have identical first drainage routes.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace nasal gland secretomotor fibers from cranial nerve to mucosa.
retrievalPrompts.answer: CN VII→greater petrosal nerve→nerve of pterygoid canal→pterygopalatine ganglion synapse→V2 branches carrying postganglionic fibers to nasal glands.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Contrast posterior and anterior nasal lymph drainage.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Posterior cavity and sinuses drain toward upper deep cervical nodes, with some lymph passing through retropharyngeal nodes; anterior regions can drain forward toward submandibular nodes.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Pharyngeal regions, isthmuses and mucosal landmarks
concepts.summary: The pharynx is a musculofascial passage from the skull base to the esophagus at approximately C6. Its three regions are named for the anterior cavity opening into them, and the soft palate changes which of these spaces communicate during breathing, chewing and swallowing.
keyPoints: Nasopharynx lies behind the choanae and above the soft palate; oropharynx lies behind the mouth, below the soft palate and above the upper epiglottic margin; laryngopharynx extends behind the larynx toward the esophagus at C6.
The pharyngeal isthmus joins nasopharynx to oropharynx. The oropharyngeal isthmus joins oral cavity to oropharynx and is bounded by the palatoglossal arches.

Elevation of the soft palate closes the pharyngeal isthmus during swallowing. Depression of the palate, tongue elevation and medial movement of the arches can instead close the oral–pharyngeal opening while material is held in the mouth.
The pharyngotympanic tube opens on the lateral nasopharyngeal wall. Its cartilaginous prominence forms the torus tubarius, with the pharyngeal recess behind it.
The salpingopharyngeal fold covers salpingopharyngeus; the torus levatorius covers levator veli palatini. A fold name therefore often identifies the underlying structure.
Valleculae are paired depressions between the tongue base and epiglottis. Piriform fossae lie lateral to the laryngeal inlet and guide a swallowed bolus around it.
The pharynx lies anterior to the vertebral column, separated from it by a retropharyngeal space. The source’s shared air/food passage should be understood together with protective laryngeal closure.
examTraps: The pharyngeal isthmus is not the oropharyngeal isthmus.
Valleculae are anterior to the epiglottis; piriform fossae are lateral to the laryngeal inlet.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Name each anterior communication of the three pharyngeal regions.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Choanae open into nasopharynx; oropharyngeal isthmus opens into oropharynx; laryngeal inlet opens into laryngopharynx.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What changes when the soft palate elevates during swallowing?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It closes the connection between nasopharynx and oropharynx, helping prevent the bolus entering the nasal airway.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Pharyngeal muscles, attachments and fascia
concepts.summary: Circular constrictors propel a bolus downward, whereas longitudinal muscles elevate the pharynx over it. Their bony/ligamentous attachments and overlapping arrangement create a supported but incomplete muscular wall, reinforced by inner and outer fascial layers.
keyPoints: Superior, middle and inferior constrictors meet posteriorly at the pharyngeal raphe. The raphe attaches superiorly at the pharyngeal tubercle of the skull base.
The superior constrictor attaches around the pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe and adjacent mandible. The pterygomandibular raphe links it to buccinator on the oral side.
The middle constrictor attaches to the hyoid horns and lower stylohyoid ligament. The inferior constrictor attaches to thyroid/cricoid structures, including the thyroid oblique line.
Inferior constrictor overlaps the lower part of middle constrictor, and middle overlaps superior. Sequential top-to-bottom contraction narrows the lumen and advances a bolus.
Stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus are the longitudinal group: their origins are respectively styloid process, pharyngotympanic tube and palatine aponeurosis.
Longitudinal contraction elevates the pharynx. Palatopharyngeus also contributes to closure of the oropharyngeal isthmus and raises the visible posterior tonsillar arch.
Buccopharyngeal fascia coats the outside of the muscular wall. Pharyngobasilar fascia is the stronger inner layer, especially important above the superior constrictor where muscle is deficient.
All pharyngeal muscles are supplied by vagal pathways except stylopharyngeus, which receives CN IX. Tables 8.17 and 8.18 organize attachments, innervation and action together.
examTraps: Constrictor contraction is not the same action as longitudinal elevation.
The outer fascial layer is buccopharyngeal; the inner supporting layer is pharyngobasilar.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Build a three-row origin map for the constrictors.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Superior: pterygoid/raphe/mandibular region; middle: hyoid and stylohyoid ligament; inferior: thyroid and cricoid cartilages. All join the posterior pharyngeal raphe.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Compare the longitudinal muscles and their motor supply.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Stylopharyngeus originates from styloid and is supplied by IX; salpingopharyngeus originates from the auditory tube and palatopharyngeus from the palate, both supplied by X. They elevate the pharynx.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Passages through the pharyngeal wall
concepts.summary: The pharyngeal wall is a set of overlapping muscles rather than an uninterrupted tube. Its gaps are consistent routes for palate muscles, stylopharyngeus and the neurovascular structures entering the larynx.
keyPoints: Above the superior constrictor, fascia completes the wall. Levator veli palatini enters the palate through this region below the auditory tube.
Tensor veli palatini takes a different route: its tendon hooks around the pterygoid hamulus before entering the palate. Do not assign the two palate muscles identical courses.
The gap between superior and middle constrictors admits stylopharyngeus and is related to the oropharyngeal triangle, bounded also by the posterior mylohyoid border.
CN IX passes around stylopharyngeus and through the superior/middle-constrictor gap toward the posterior tongue. Its proximity to the palatine tonsil matters for regional anatomy.
Between middle and inferior constrictors, the internal laryngeal nerve and accompanying superior laryngeal vessels reach the thyrohyoid membrane.
Below the inferior constrictor, the recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior laryngeal vessels enter behind the inferior thyroid horn. This is a separate entry from the thyrohyoid route.
examTraps: The internal laryngeal nerve does not enter below the inferior constrictor with the recurrent nerve.
Stylopharyngeus does not pass between middle and inferior constrictors.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Reconstruct the four levels of passage around the constrictors.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Above superior: palatal/tubal region; superior–middle: stylopharyngeus and IX-related passage; middle–inferior: internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels; below inferior: recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior laryngeal vessels.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does the thyrohyoid-membrane route differ from the inferior entry to the larynx?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The first is reached between middle and inferior constrictors by the internal superior-laryngeal branch; the second lies deep to the inferior constrictor and carries recurrent laryngeal structures.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Tonsils and pharyngeal vascular–lymphatic routes
concepts.summary: The largest pharyngeal lymphoid collections surround the nasal and oral entrances, but their positions and drainage are different. The palatine tonsil is especially useful for linking a visible oral landmark to a deep muscle, artery and cervical node.
keyPoints: Pharyngeal tonsil lies in the nasopharyngeal roof and is called adenoids when enlarged. Enlargement can obstruct the nasal airway without being a palatine-tonsil lesion.
Palatine tonsils lie between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches on the lateral oropharyngeal walls, over the superior constrictor.
Lingual tonsils are collections on the posterior third of the tongue. Smaller lymphoid collections also occur near the auditory-tube openings and upper palate.

The major palatine-tonsil arterial supply is the tonsillar branch of the facial artery, which pierces the superior constrictor. Ascending pharyngeal, palatine, maxillary and lingual branches also contribute to regional pharyngeal supply.
Lower pharyngeal supply includes inferior-thyroid branches from the thyrocervical/subclavian system, rather than being exclusively external carotid.
Pharyngeal veins form a plexus draining toward the pterygoid plexus superiorly and facial/internal jugular veins inferiorly.
Pharyngeal lymph reaches deep cervical pathways, including retropharyngeal, paratracheal and infrahyoid nodes. Palatine-tonsil lymph is particularly associated with jugulodigastric nodes.
examTraps: Adenoids are enlarged pharyngeal tonsil, not another name for palatine tonsils.
Jugulodigastric drainage is a tonsillar association; it is not the only node for every pharyngeal region.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Locate the pharyngeal, palatine and lingual tonsils.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Roof of nasopharynx; lateral oropharynx between the two tonsillar arches; posterior third of tongue, respectively.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace the dominant palatine-tonsil artery and lymph route.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Facial artery→tonsillar branch through superior constrictor; lymph passes through the pharyngeal wall toward jugulodigastric nodes.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Pharyngeal sensory territories and reflex pathways
concepts.summary: A regional V2–IX–X pattern organizes pharyngeal sensation from superior to inferior. Motor innervation is predominantly vagal, with the isolated stylopharyngeus exception; mixing sensory territory and motor supply is a common source of errors.
keyPoints: Nasopharyngeal general sensation travels in a pharyngeal branch of V2 from the pterygopalatine region.
Oropharyngeal sensation, including palatine-tonsil sensation, is mainly through CN IX and the pharyngeal plexus.
Laryngopharyngeal sensation is vagal, particularly through the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
The pharyngeal plexus lies in the outer fascia of the pharyngeal wall and receives vagal and glossopharyngeal contributions; the pharyngeal vagal branch is its major motor component.
Stylopharyngeus receives a direct motor branch from CN IX. Its motor exception does not mean the other longitudinal muscles are also glossopharyngeal.
CN IX carries the afferent limb of the gag reflex from the oropharynx. Regional sensory testing and motor movement must be interpreted as different parts of a pathway.
examTraps: CN IX is not the general sensory nerve of the nasopharynx.
A nerve serving an afferent reflex limb does not automatically supply all muscles producing the response.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Give the superior-to-inferior sensory sequence for the pharynx.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Nasopharynx V2; oropharynx IX; laryngopharynx X through the internal superior-laryngeal branch.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why can the glossopharyngeal nerve be tested both by pharyngeal sensation and by one muscle exception?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It supplies oropharyngeal sensory afferents and separately supplies stylopharyngeus motor fibers; these are distinct functions of the same nerve.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Laryngeal cartilages and attachment landmarks
concepts.summary: The larynx combines a rigid but movable cartilage framework with membranes and muscles. Its posterior arytenoids act as mobile anchors for the vocal ligaments, while the complete cricoid ring supports the lower airway and articulations.
keyPoints: Unpaired cartilages are thyroid, cricoid and epiglottis; paired cartilages are arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform. The hyoid suspends the larynx but is a bone, not one of its cartilages.

The thyroid has two laminae meeting anteriorly, a palpable prominence and notch, superior/inferior horns and an oblique line for extrinsic muscle attachments. The book illustrates a more acute typical male thyroid angle, not an invariant diagnostic measurement.
The cricoid completely encircles the airway: narrow arch anteriorly, broad lamina posteriorly. Its posterior depressions give attachment to posterior cricoarytenoid muscles.
Cricoid facets articulate with the bases of arytenoids superiorly and the inferior thyroid horns laterally. The thyroid’s superior horns instead relate to the hyoid through ligaments.
Each arytenoid has an anterior vocal process for the vocal ligament and a lateral muscular process for posterior/lateral cricoarytenoid attachments.
Corniculate cartilages articulate with arytenoid apices. Cuneiform cartilages are suspended more anteriorly in the aryepiglottic fold region rather than sitting directly on those apices.

The epiglottic stem attaches to the thyroid angle through the thyroepiglottic ligament; the hyoepiglottic ligament connects it to the hyoid. Its position relates the tongue base to the laryngeal inlet.
examTraps: The muscular process, not the vocal process, is the cricoarytenoid muscle attachment.
Cricoid is a complete ring; thyroid laminae are widely separated posteriorly.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Compare vocal and muscular arytenoid processes.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The anterior vocal process anchors the vocal ligament; the lateral muscular process receives posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How do the corniculate and cuneiform positions differ?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Corniculate lies on an arytenoid apex; cuneiform is suspended anterior to it in the fold/membrane leading toward the epiglottis.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Intrinsic membranes and extrinsic ligaments
concepts.summary: The fibroelastic framework provides two different pairs of free margins: vocal ligaments below and vestibular ligaments above. External connections suspend the larynx and transmit neurovascular structures, so the thyrohyoid and cricothyroid intervals should not be conflated.
keyPoints: The lower fibroelastic component, called conus elasticus or cricovocal/cricothyroid membrane, attaches to the cricoid and has a thickened upper free margin forming the vocal ligament.
Each vocal ligament runs from the thyroid angle anteriorly to the arytenoid vocal process posteriorly and lies within the true vocal fold.
The quadrangular membrane extends from the epiglottis toward arytenoid/corniculate structures. Its lower free margin forms the vestibular ligament within the false vocal fold.
The upper free margin of the quadrangular membrane supports the aryepiglottic fold. This fold belongs to the inlet boundary, not the vocal ligament below.
Viewed from above, vestibular ligaments lie lateral to vocal ligaments because of their different arytenoid attachments. The interval between them allows the laryngeal ventricle to extend laterally.
The thyrohyoid membrane joins thyroid cartilage to hyoid and is pierced laterally by internal superior-laryngeal nerve, superior laryngeal vessels and lymphatics.
The median cricothyroid ligament spans the anterior thyroid–cricoid interval; the cricotracheal ligament links cricoid to the first tracheal cartilage. These are separate anatomical levels.
The book’s emergency-airway box identifies the median cricothyroid interval. Here it is studied as a landmark only, not as instructions or a current procedural recommendation.
examTraps: Conus elasticus gives the vocal ligament; quadrangular membrane gives the vestibular ligament.
The thyrohyoid membrane is above the thyroid cartilage, not between thyroid and cricoid.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace the free margins of the two intrinsic membranes.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Conus elasticus: upper margin→vocal ligament. Quadrangular membrane: lower margin→vestibular ligament; upper margin→aryepiglottic fold.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Differentiate the thyrohyoid, cricothyroid and cricotracheal intervals.
retrievalPrompts.answer: They join hyoid–thyroid, thyroid–cricoid and cricoid–first tracheal cartilage, respectively.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Laryngeal inlet, chambers, ventricles and saccules
concepts.summary: The laryngeal lumen has three vertical regions separated by two pairs of folds. The lateral ventricle and its gland-bearing saccule are extensions between these folds rather than alternative names for the central airway.
keyPoints: The inlet is bounded anteriorly by epiglottis, laterally by aryepiglottic folds and posteriorly by the interarytenoid region between the corniculate tubercles.
The vestibule extends from inlet to vestibular folds. The middle chamber lies between vestibular folds above and vocal folds below.
The infraglottic cavity extends from vocal folds to the lower laryngeal opening at the cricoid, where it continues into the trachea.
The rima vestibuli is the opening between vestibular folds. The narrower rima glottidis is bounded by vocal folds and adjacent arytenoid-related mucosa.
A laryngeal ventricle projects laterally from the middle chamber between vestibular and vocal folds. It is paired, unlike the single central airway lumen.
Each saccule projects anterosuperiorly from a ventricle between vestibular fold and thyroid cartilage. Its glands provide mucus that lubricates vocal folds.
In laryngoscopic orientation the epiglottis is anterior and the arytenoid/interarytenoid region posterior. Fold identity should be judged by their arrangement, not merely their color in a photograph.
examTraps: The saccule is an extension of a ventricle, not the infraglottic airway.
The laryngeal vestibule and rima vestibuli are a chamber and an opening, respectively.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Describe the three chambers from superior to inferior.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Vestibule above vestibular folds; middle chamber between vestibular and vocal folds; infraglottic cavity below vocal folds to the cricoid-level opening.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Where is the laryngeal saccule and why does it matter?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It extends anterosuperiorly from a lateral ventricle between vestibular fold and thyroid cartilage; its mucus-producing glands lubricate vocal folds.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Intrinsic muscles opening and closing the airway
concepts.summary: Arytenoid rotation and approximation move the vocal folds. Posterior and lateral cricoarytenoids pull on the same muscular process from different directions, while transverse/oblique arytenoids act across the posterior framework.
keyPoints: Posterior cricoarytenoid originates on posterior cricoid lamina and inserts on the arytenoid muscular process. Its lateral rotation/abduction opens the rima glottidis; it is the primary vocal-fold abductor.
Lateral cricoarytenoid originates from the upper cricoid arch and reaches the muscular process from anteriorly. It rotates the arytenoid medially, adducting the vocal fold.
Transverse arytenoid is the unpaired muscle spanning the posterior surfaces of the arytenoid cartilages; it brings them together.
Oblique arytenoids cross from a muscular process toward the opposite apex. Continuing aryepiglottic fibers contribute to narrowing the laryngeal inlet.
Thyroarytenoid lies lateral to the fibroelastic membrane and lateral cavity extensions. In the scoped Gray description it compresses the vestibule and helps narrow the inlet.
These muscles receive recurrent-laryngeal motor supply. A posterior-view identification of one muscle is only a visual sample, not proof that its action or nerve supply has also been tested.
Table 8.19 links origins and insertions with action: the direction of pull explains why “cricoarytenoid” does not imply that both named muscles have the same effect.
examTraps: Posterior cricoarytenoid abducts; lateral cricoarytenoid adducts.
Transverse arytenoid is unpaired, whereas oblique arytenoids form a paired crossing arrangement.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain why posterior and lateral cricoarytenoids have opposite actions.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Both attach to the muscular process, but the posterior muscle pulls from the cricoid lamina to rotate the arytenoid laterally, whereas the lateral muscle approaches from the arch and rotates it medially.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which intrinsic muscles narrow the inlet beyond simply adducting vocal folds?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Oblique arytenoid/aryepiglottic fibers and thyroarytenoid-associated fibers contribute to narrowing the inlet and vestibule.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Laryngeal joints and control of vocal-fold tension
concepts.summary: Laryngeal joints convert muscle pull into changes in both vocal-fold position and length. Cricothyroid motion changes the distance between thyroid and arytenoid anchors, while vocalis adjusts tension along the fold more locally.
keyPoints: The cricothyroid joints are synovial articulations between inferior thyroid horns and lateral cricoid facets.
Forward/downward tilt of the thyroid relative to cricoid increases the distance from the thyroid angle to arytenoid vocal processes, lengthening and tensing the vocal ligaments.
Cricothyroid originates on the anterolateral cricoid arch, with straight and oblique parts reaching the inferior thyroid margin and inferior horn.
The cricoarytenoid joints are also synovial and permit rotation and sliding. These movements alter arytenoid separation and the width of the glottic opening.
Vocalis runs next to the vocal ligament and attaches along it, allowing adjustment of vocal-fold tension rather than merely moving the whole larynx.
Cricothyroid is the intrinsic-muscle motor exception supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. Vocalis receives recurrent-laryngeal supply.
examTraps: Cricothyroid movement tensions the folds; it is not the main vocal-fold abduction mechanism.
A cricoarytenoid joint and a cricothyroid joint involve different partners and movements.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain vocal-fold tension using the two ligament attachment points.
retrievalPrompts.answer: The vocal ligament spans thyroid angle to arytenoid vocal process; thyroid tilt increases their separation and tensions the ligament.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does vocalis differ from cricothyroid?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Vocalis adjusts tension along the vocal fold and is recurrent-laryngeal supplied; cricothyroid acts across a joint to lengthen the fold and is external superior-laryngeal supplied.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Respiration, phonation, effort closure and swallowing
concepts.summary: The larynx can be an open airway, a sound-producing valve or a protective sphincter. These are different coordinated configurations of the same folds, arytenoids, inlet and extrinsic suspensory apparatus.
keyPoints: During quiet breathing the laryngeal inlet, vestibule and both rimae are open. The rima glottidis is roughly triangular.
Forced inspiration produces greater arytenoid abduction/lateral rotation and a wider, roughly rhomboid glottic opening, prominently through posterior cricoarytenoid action.
Phonation approximates the vocal folds so passing air makes them vibrate; vocalis and cricothyroid modify tension. The vestibule remains open in the source’s phonation diagram.
Effort closure retains air by closing the rima glottidis and rima vestibuli, with closure of the lower vestibule. It therefore involves more than merely adjusting pitch.
Swallowing closes the vocal and vestibular openings, narrows the inlet and moves the larynx upward and forward. Epiglottic movement is part of this coordinated protection, not an isolated lid action.
The upward/forward movement also facilitates esophageal opening behind the cricoid. Piriform fossae guide material around the elevated laryngeal inlet.

Extrinsic muscles move the larynx as a whole through attachments to it or the hyoid; intrinsic muscles change its lumen and folds. Suprahyoid/infrahyoid illustrations should be read with that functional distinction.

Laryngoscopy exposes inlet and fold relationships; tracheostomy bypasses part of the upper airway. Historical clinical boxes are used for anatomical orientation, not contemporary technique or management advice.
examTraps: Phonation and effort closure do not require the same vestibular configuration.
Swallowing protection includes elevation and multiple levels of closure, not just the epiglottis.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Contrast phonation and effort closure.
retrievalPrompts.answer: In phonation vocal folds approximate and vibrate while the vestibule remains open; effort closure tightly closes vocal and vestibular levels to retain air.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: List the protective changes during swallowing.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Larynx rises and moves forward; vocal/vestibular openings close; inlet narrows as epiglottis moves toward arytenoids; the bolus passes through piriform channels toward the opening esophagus.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Laryngeal sensory boundaries, motor exceptions and recurrent courses
concepts.summary: Two vagal branches divide the larynx into clinically useful sensory and motor territories. The recurrent nerves also take different right and left courses, so a thoracic or thyroid-region lesion can affect the voice even without a primary lesion of the vocal fold.
keyPoints: The superior laryngeal nerve divides into an internal, mainly sensory branch and an external, principally motor branch.
Internal superior-laryngeal nerve passes through the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery and supplies the cavity down to the vocal-fold level.
External superior-laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid and contributes to inferior-constrictor supply. Injury can impair tension control while leaving recurrent-supplied muscles intact.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, and sensation below the vocal folds.
Right recurrent laryngeal nerve turns around the right subclavian artery in the root of the neck; left recurrent laryngeal nerve turns around the aortic arch in the thorax.
Both ascend toward the larynx in the tracheoesophageal groove and enter deep to the inferior constrictor, behind the inferior thyroid horn.
Relations to the thyroid’s lateral ligament are variable. Voice change with preserved cricothyroid function points to a different pattern than an isolated external superior-laryngeal injury.

The lecture includes an internal-laryngeal block diagram and a unilateral-paralysis view. The source-grounded objective is nerve location/territory; injection technique and fixed vocal-fold positions in every lesion are not inferred.
examTraps: Internal superior-laryngeal is not the motor nerve to cricothyroid.
A recurrent lesion spares cricothyroid but not posterior cricoarytenoid.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Map superior-laryngeal internal/external branches and recurrent nerve to function.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Internal: sensation to fold level; external: cricothyroid motor; recurrent: other intrinsic muscles and sensation below folds.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why can a left thoracic lesion affect the voice?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The left recurrent nerve loops under the aortic arch before ascending in the neck, placing part of its course within the thorax.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Laryngeal arteries, veins and regional lymphatic drainage
concepts.summary: Superior and inferior laryngeal neurovascular routes enter at different levels and arise from different arterial systems. Venous and lymphatic drainage are similarly regional; the vocal folds provide a useful boundary without making all glottic tissue equivalent to the supraglottis.
keyPoints: Superior laryngeal artery arises from superior thyroid artery, an external-carotid branch. It crosses the thyrohyoid membrane with the internal superior-laryngeal nerve.
Inferior laryngeal artery arises from inferior thyroid artery of the thyrocervical trunk. It ascends with the recurrent nerve and enters below the inferior constrictor.
Superior laryngeal veins drain through superior thyroid veins to internal jugular veins.
Inferior laryngeal veins drain through inferior thyroid veins toward the left brachiocephalic vein in the scoped book description.
Above the vocal folds, lymph follows the superior laryngeal arterial route toward deep cervical nodes near the common-carotid bifurcation.
Below the vocal folds, lymph reaches deep nodes associated with the inferior thyroid artery and anterior cricothyroid/upper-tracheal nodes.

The lecture loosely groups the cords with the upper region in one caption; the notes and questions deliberately say “above the folds” to match the book and avoid claiming identical drainage of the folds themselves.
examTraps: Superior laryngeal artery is not a branch of inferior thyroid artery.
A nerve and vessel sharing an entry route need not have matching “superior/inferior” word stems: internal superior-laryngeal nerve travels with superior laryngeal artery.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace the two laryngeal arterial routes from their parent vessels.
retrievalPrompts.answer: External carotid→superior thyroid→superior laryngeal through thyrohyoid membrane; subclavian→thyrocervical→inferior thyroid→inferior laryngeal below inferior constrictor.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Compare lymph drainage above and below vocal folds.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Above: along superior laryngeal artery to deep cervical nodes near carotid bifurcation. Below: toward inferior-thyroid-associated and prelaryngeal/upper-tracheal nodes.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Trachea, carina and main bronchi
concepts.summary: The trachea connects the cricoid-level airway in the neck with the two main bronchi in the mediastinum. Its posterior flexibility, anterior thyroid relationship and asymmetrical bronchial branching explain several basic clinical-anatomy observations.
keyPoints: The trachea begins around C6 and bifurcates around the T4/T5 disc plane, near the sternal-angle reference plane. Vertebral landmarks are approximate anatomical conventions, not fixed positions in every posture or respiratory phase.
C-shaped cartilage rings keep the lumen open. Their open ends face posteriorly, where smooth muscle forms much of the wall next to the esophagus.

The thyroid isthmus crosses the anterior cervical trachea in the illustrated upper-ring region. A lower anterior neck approach can therefore encounter thyroid tissue before reaching tracheal cartilage.
The carina is the internal ridge between the main bronchial origins. In bronchoscopy it is a branching landmark, not a separate bronchial tube.
The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical than the left; inhaled foreign bodies therefore more often enter the right bronchial tree.

Each main bronchus travels through a lung root and hilum. The right superior lobar bronchus arises within the root, an important exception to simply imagining all lobar branches arising deep inside the lung.

The lecture includes neighboring thyroid and great-vessel diagrams; the respiratory core is to locate airway, esophagus and important overlying structures. Detailed cardiac plexus anatomy is excluded from this respiratory module.
examTraps: The esophagus is posterior, not anterior, to the tracheal membranous wall.
The carina is a ridge at the bifurcation, not the right main bronchus.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace the airway from cricoid to main bronchi using landmarks.
retrievalPrompts.answer: It begins near C6, descends in front of the esophagus, and divides near T4/T5; the carina lies between the main bronchial openings.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What features favor aspiration into the right bronchus?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Its larger caliber and more vertical course compared with the left main bronchus.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Bronchial hierarchy and bronchopulmonary segments
concepts.summary: Bronchi branch into lobar and then segmental territories, allowing the lung to be understood as a set of functional surgical units. Segmental bronchi and pulmonary arteries travel together within a unit, while pulmonary venous tributaries tend to mark its margins.
keyPoints: Main bronchi supply lungs, lobar/secondary bronchi supply lobes, and segmental/tertiary bronchi supply bronchopulmonary segments. The normal lobar count is three on the right and two on the left.
A segment is roughly conical: its apex faces the origin of its segmental bronchus near the hilum and its base projects toward the lung surface.
A segmental bronchus and accompanying pulmonary-artery branch supply the segment. Pulmonary-vein tributaries generally pass between and around segment boundaries.
This arrangement makes a segment the smallest functionally independent lung region described as separately resectable without removing neighboring regions.
Right superior lobe: apical S1, posterior S2, anterior S3. Right middle lobe: lateral S4 and medial S5. Right inferior lobe: superior S6 and medial/anterior/lateral/posterior basal S7/S8/S9/S10.

Left superior lobe includes an apicoposterior S1+2, anterior S3 and superior/inferior lingular S4/S5 pattern. The left inferior lobe has superior S6 and basal territories; some segments fuse on the left.

Gray’s convention describes ten segmental territories with some left-sided fusion. Do not make an unqualified “exactly eight in every left lung” claim or infer a variant solely from a simplified picture.
Bronchi have cartilage plates; bronchioles lack cartilage. Distal histologic subdivisions are developed in the histology module rather than replacing these gross-anatomical units.
examTraps: The superior segment belongs to an inferior lobe; “superior segment” is not “superior lobe.”
Pulmonary arteries accompany segmental bronchi; pulmonary veins commonly run intersegmentally.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Reconstruct the right segment list by lobe.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Superior: apical, posterior, anterior; middle: lateral, medial; inferior: superior plus medial, anterior, lateral and posterior basal territories.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why can a segment be separated anatomically from its neighbor?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It has its own segmental bronchus and accompanying arterial branch, with venous tributaries generally between segments; this creates a functional territorial unit.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Lung surfaces, fissures and chest-wall projection
concepts.summary: Lobes are not stacked as simple horizontal blocks. Their oblique fissures place much of the inferior lobes against the posterior chest, whereas the right middle lobe and left lingula are more anterior structures.
keyPoints: Each lung has an apex extending into the root of the neck, a diaphragmatic base, a costal surface and a medial/mediastinal surface. The posterior border is more rounded than the sharp anterior and inferior borders.
Right lung has superior, middle and inferior lobes separated by horizontal and oblique fissures. The horizontal fissure separates superior from middle lobe; the oblique separates inferior from both.
Left lung has superior and inferior lobes separated by an oblique fissure. Its cardiac notch and lingula belong to the superior-lobe/anterior-border region; lingula is not a third left lobe.
Inferior lobes occupy much of the posterior and inferior thoracic wall. Right middle lobe is chiefly related to the lower anterior/lateral chest, so posterior listening alone poorly samples it.
An oblique fissure projects from about the T4 spinous region posteriorly, crosses the fifth interspace laterally and reaches the sixth-rib contour anteriorly. These are approximate surface guides.

The right horizontal fissure approaches the fourth-rib/costal-cartilage region anteriorly and meets the oblique fissure laterally. Surface descriptions are not perfectly identical between the prose and figure captions; learn the region rather than a false millimeter precision.
The right medial surface is related to SVC, IVC and azygos arch, among other structures; the left is related to aortic arch and descending thoracic aorta. Both have cardiac and esophageal relations.
The slide’s azygos-lobe variant shows an atypical azygos course drawing a pleural fold into the apical right lung. It is a variant appearance and must not replace the ordinary three-lobe description.

Chest radiography and cross-sectional CT localize findings relative to lobes, roots and neighboring structures. The book’s high-resolution-CT box concerns detailed lung/interstitial localization; scanner settings, diagnosis and modality selection are not learning targets here.
examTraps: The right middle lobe is predominantly anterior/lateral, not posterior lower lung.
Lingula is part of the left superior lobe; an azygos-lobe image is a variant, not the standard fourth lobe.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain where to assess the right middle and inferior lobes anatomically.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Middle lobe is most exposed to anterior/lateral chest-wall assessment; inferior lobe has extensive posterior and inferior costal surfaces.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Name a mediastinal impression that distinguishes each side.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Right: azygos/SVC-related grooves; left: aortic arch/descending aortic groove. Both may show heart and esophageal impressions.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Roots, hila and pulmonary ligaments
concepts.summary: The root is the short bundle connecting lung and mediastinum; the hilum is its gateway on the medial lung surface. Pleural reflection around that bundle and asymmetric bronchovascular ordering make orientation essential when interpreting a root diagram.
keyPoints: A root contains a bronchus, pulmonary artery, two pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves and lymphatics. Its pleural sleeve reflects into visceral pleura at the hilum.
Pulmonary veins tend to lie anteriorly/inferiorly and bronchi more posteriorly. The relationship of artery to bronchus differs between sides and should be read with view orientation.
The right superior lobar bronchus lies above the pulmonary artery: the eparterial bronchus. Do not assume that every superior structure in the right root is an artery.
On the left, the pulmonary artery arches above the bronchus. The right pulmonary artery courses anterior to the right main bronchus as it approaches the root.
Phrenic nerve passes anterior to each root; vagus passes posterior. These are neighboring mediastinal routes, not two interchangeable elements entering the lung in the same way.
The pulmonary ligament is a double pleural fold extending inferiorly from the root toward the mediastinum. It allows accommodation of root movement and is not an artery or bronchus.

The supplied right-root image target is intentionally labeled “right bronchus,” not forced to a main-versus-lobar subtype that the crop cannot establish. Identification coverage is limited to that defensible label.
examTraps: Root and hilum are related but not synonymous structures.
The right superior lobar bronchus is above the artery; this is not the usual left-root order.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Describe the nerve relationships to a lung root.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Phrenic is anterior and vagus posterior to the root.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the pulmonary ligament continuous with?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The pleural sleeve around the root; it is an inferior pleural fold linking hilum/root region to mediastinum.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Pulmonary and bronchial circulations
concepts.summary: The lung has an exchange circulation from the right heart and a nutritive systemic circulation for its supporting tissues. Both use the root, but their origins, oxygen content and venous outlets are not identical.
keyPoints: Pulmonary trunk divides into right and left pulmonary arteries that carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs.
The right pulmonary artery is longer and crosses the mediastinum anterior to the right main bronchus and posterior to the ascending aorta and SVC.
The left pulmonary artery is shorter, lies anterior to descending aorta and posterior to the superior pulmonary vein, and arches superior to the left bronchus at the root.
Superior and inferior pulmonary veins on each side return oxygenated blood to the left atrium. Artery/vein naming follows direction relative to heart, not oxygen content.
Bronchial arteries nourish bronchial walls/glands, walls of large pulmonary vessels and visceral pleura. They arise from the thoracic aorta or its branches.
The usual book pattern is one right bronchial artery from the third posterior intercostal artery and two left bronchial arteries directly from thoracic aorta; variations occur.
Bronchial arteries run on posterior bronchial surfaces and connect with pulmonary vessels. Bronchial venous return includes pulmonary veins/left atrium and systemic azygos-related outlets.

Right systemic bronchial venous drainage reaches azygos; left may reach superior intercostal or hemiazygos routes. Therefore “all bronchial venous blood directly enters the right heart” is too absolute.
examTraps: Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood despite being arteries.
Bronchial supply is nutritive; it is not a substitute for pulmonary exchange flow.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace pulmonary flow through the heart–lung circuit.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Right ventricle→pulmonary trunk→pulmonary arteries→lung exchange vessels→pulmonary veins→left atrium.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Give the usual bronchial artery pattern and explain why it is a convention.
retrievalPrompts.answer: One right from the third posterior intercostal and two left from thoracic aorta is the book’s usual pattern; it explicitly allows variant origins.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Pulmonary plexuses and visceral innervation
concepts.summary: Vagal and sympathetic fibers reach the lung through interconnected plexuses near the main bronchi. These regulate airway caliber and carry visceral information, whereas nearby phrenic and intercostal pathways serve different somatic structures.
keyPoints: Anterior and posterior pulmonary plexuses lie around the tracheal bifurcation and main bronchi; the posterior plexus is larger in the scoped description.
The plexuses receive branches from vagus nerves and sympathetic trunks. Their branches distribute along airways and pulmonary vessels.
Vagal efferents constrict bronchioles; sympathetic efferents dilate them. This is an anatomical autonomic distinction, not a replacement for the physiology of receptor signaling.
Lung structures and visceral pleura receive visceral afferent/efferent pathways through these plexuses.
Phrenic nerve passing anterior to the root is not the motor supply of bronchial smooth muscle. Its major respiratory motor target is the diaphragm.
Somatic pain from parietal pleura must be distinguished from visceral innervation of the lung and visceral pleura. The same word “pleura” does not imply one common nerve supply.
examTraps: Vagus constricts rather than dilates bronchioles in the book’s efferent summary.
Phrenic–root proximity is not evidence that phrenic controls bronchial caliber.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace autonomic fibers into the lung.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Vagus and sympathetic-trunk branches form anterior/posterior pulmonary plexuses, then distribute along airway and vessel branches.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Contrast vagal and sympathetic effects on bronchioles.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Vagal efferents constrict; sympathetic efferents dilate.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Pulmonary lymphatic routes and anatomical spread
concepts.summary: Superficial and deep lymphatics link the lung to hilar, tracheobronchial and neck-root pathways. The route is useful for understanding anatomical spread, but a simple diagram is not a full map of cancer staging or every possible cross-drainage variant.
keyPoints: Superficial/subpleural lymphatics and deep pulmonary lymphatics both contribute to drainage toward the root and tracheobronchial node groups.
The lecture identifies bronchopulmonary/hilar, inferior tracheobronchial (subcarinal) and paratracheal nodes. Their names describe positions along the branching airway.
Efferents ascend along the trachea and join drainage from other thoracic nodes to form bronchomediastinal trunks.

Bronchomediastinal trunks may drain directly into deep veins at the neck base or join the right lymphatic pathway/thoracic duct. A mandatory single final duct on each side should not be imposed on the book’s variable description.

The clinical lung-cancer box emphasizes lymph spread to hilar, mediastinal and root-of-neck nodes and direct relationships to mediastinum/pleura. Management algorithms and staging systems are outside these notes.
Pulmonary lymphatic drainage is not a complete account of pleural-fluid resorption. The eleven decks do not establish a detailed parietal-pleural stomatal pathway or drainage procedure.
examTraps: Subcarinal nodes are inferior to the tracheal bifurcation, not identical to every paratracheal node.
A bronchomediastinal trunk need not always end through one obligatory named duct.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace pulmonary lymph from lung to neck root.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Superficial/deep lung lymph→hilar/tracheobronchial groups→ascending efferents→bronchomediastinal trunks→deep neck-base veins or a major lymphatic duct pathway.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What does a subcarinal node name tell you?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It locates an inferior tracheobronchial node beneath the carina, near the main bronchial origins.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Pleural layers, cervical cupola and continuity at the hilum
concepts.summary: Parietal and visceral pleura are continuous surfaces enclosing a normally thin potential space. The parietal layer is named for the wall it lines; the visceral layer follows the lung even into its fissures.
keyPoints: Parietal pleura lines thoracic boundaries; visceral pleura adheres to lung and covers the opposed surfaces within lobar fissures.
The pleural cavity lies between them and normally contains only a thin serous-fluid film, permitting sliding during respiratory movement.
Parietal subdivisions are costal, diaphragmatic, mediastinal and cervical. “Diaphragmatic pleura” denotes a pleural surface, not the diaphragm muscle itself.
Mediastinal pleura reflects around the root and becomes visceral at the hilum. An inferior continuation of that sleeve forms the pulmonary ligament.
Cervical pleura/cupola extends above the first rib into the root of the neck. Its height relative to first costal cartilage differs from its relation to the posterior neck of rib 1.
The suprapleural membrane supports the cupola, attaching to the medial first-rib margin and C7 transverse process; scalene-associated fibers help maintain its tension.
The two pleural sacs lie to either side of the mediastinum. A unilateral pleural-space process is not initially an opening into one common sac around both lungs.
examTraps: Pleura in the fissures is visceral, not a new parietal compartment.
The cervical cupola is not capped at the horizontal level of the first costal cartilage.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Describe pleural continuity at the root.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Mediastinal parietal pleura sleeves the root and reflects onto the lung as visceral pleura; the sleeve’s inferior extension forms pulmonary ligament.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What supports the cervical pleural dome?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The suprapleural membrane, anchored to medial rib 1 and C7 transverse process.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Pleural recesses and inferior surface landmarks
concepts.summary: The lung does not fill every part of its pleural sac during quiet respiration. Recesses occur where parietal surfaces oppose one another, and their size changes as the lung border moves with breathing.
keyPoints: The costodiaphragmatic recess lies between costal and diaphragmatic pleura below the inferior lung border. It is the largest pleural recess and a potential dependent fluid-collection region.
Costomediastinal recesses lie anteriorly between costal and mediastinal pleura; the larger left recess relates to the heart’s displacement of the anterior lung margin.
The quiet-respiration lung margin follows approximately rib 6 at midclavicular line, rib 8 at midaxillary line and T10 posteriorly.
The inferior pleural reflection extends farther: approximately rib 8 midclavicular, rib 10 midaxillary and T12 posteriorly. The posterior number is a vertebral level in the scoped text.
During expiration the inferior lung edge rises, enlarging the costodiaphragmatic recess. Forced inspiration expands lung into it and makes the recess shallower.
Anterior pleural reflections approach behind the upper sternum but diverge more on the left inferiorly because of the heart/pericardium.
The anatomical space that can collect fluid does not itself prescribe a safe aspiration site. Clinical positioning, imaging and technique are beyond this source-grounded anatomy resource.
examTraps: Lung border 6–8–10 and pleural border 8–10–12 are different contours.
Posterior T10/T12 should not be silently rewritten as anterior rib levels.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Reproduce lung and pleural contours at the three reference positions.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Lung: rib6 midclavicular, rib8 midaxillary, T10 posterior. Pleura: rib8 midclavicular, rib10 midaxillary, T12 posterior.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How do the recesses change during expiration?
retrievalPrompts.answer: As the lung margin rises, the costodiaphragmatic recess becomes larger/deeper.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Pleural pain, effusion and pneumothorax
concepts.summary: Pleural disease depends on both the space involved and the innervation of the affected surface. Parietal irritation can generate localized or referred pain, while air or excess fluid in the potential space mechanically compromises the adjacent lung.
keyPoints: Costal parietal pleura receives intercostal somatic afferents, producing pain referred to the corresponding thoracic wall.

Mediastinal and diaphragmatic parietal pleura are described as mainly phrenic supplied in the scoped Gray section. Phrenic C3–C5 afferents explain referral toward lateral neck and supraclavicular shoulder.
Visceral pleura receives visceral afferents accompanying bronchial vessels; ordinary pain is generally not elicited from it in the book’s comparison.
Pleural effusion is excess fluid in the pleural space, not fluid inside the bronchial lumen. Increasing volume can compress or collapse underlying lung.
Pneumothorax is air in the pleural space; loss of normal apposition allows elastic lung recoil and collapse.
In a tension pattern, accumulating pleural air can displace the mediastinum away and compromise the opposite side. The anatomy explains urgency, but treatment instructions are not provided here.
Distinguish the site of pain, the neural pathway and the pleural space involved before assigning a cause. Neither a shoulder symptom nor an image alone proves a particular diagnosis.
examTraps: Visceral pleura is not pain-sensitive in the same way as costal parietal pleura.
Air in a bronchus is normal; air between pleural layers is pneumothorax.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why can mediastinal pleural irritation be felt near the shoulder?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Its phrenic afferents enter C3–C5 levels, creating referred sensation in the associated neck/supraclavicular territory.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Contrast mechanical effects of effusion and pneumothorax.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Fluid can compress the adjacent lung; pleural air permits elastic recoil/collapse and, if under tension, can displace the mediastinum.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Intercostal framework and rib movements
concepts.summary: Breathing changes thoracic dimensions through both rib movement and diaphragmatic movement. The intercostal layers stabilize the spaces and move ribs, while the costal groove and muscle-plane relationships organize the thoracic wall’s neurovascular bundle.
keyPoints: External, internal and innermost intercostals are ordered from superficial to deep. External fibers run anteroinferiorly; internal/innermost fibers run in the opposite, posteroinferior direction in a lateral view.
The main intercostal neurovascular bundle runs between internal and innermost layers near the inferior border of the rib above. Its superior-to-inferior order is vein, artery, nerve.
Collateral branches can lie near the superior border of the rib below. The main bundle’s position therefore does not make the rest of an interspace devoid of neurovascular structures.
Endothoracic fascia separates the inner thoracic wall from parietal pleura. The innermost layer is not itself the pleural membrane.

The source table describes external intercostals as most active during inspiration and internal intercostals during expiration; all reinforce interspaces, and innermost muscles act with internal intercostals.

Subcostales span more than one interspace posteriorly; transversus thoracis lies deep on the anterior chest wall and helps depress costal cartilages. Table 3.2 organizes their attachments and related intercostal innervation.
Pump-handle rib/sternal elevation increases anteroposterior diameter. Bucket-handle elevation of lateral rib shafts increases transverse diameter.
A mobile flail segment after multiple rib fractures can move paradoxically during inspiration, impairing full expansion. The book’s anatomy is retained without procedural trauma advice.
These detailed mechanics are book-only in this payload: the respiratory decks show chest-wall landmarks but do not explicitly teach the full intercostal action table or pump/bucket-handle mechanisms.
examTraps: The main intercostal bundle lies between internal and innermost, not between external and internal.
Pump handle changes AP dimension; bucket handle changes lateral dimension.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Reconstruct an interspace from superficial muscles to pleura.
retrievalPrompts.answer: External→internal→neurovascular plane→innermost→endothoracic fascia→parietal pleura. The main bundle lies at the costal groove and has VAN ordering.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the two named rib movements in three dimensions.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Elevation of anterior rib ends moves sternum up/forward, increasing AP diameter; elevation of lateral shafts moves them outward, increasing transverse diameter.

objectives.text: Locate the main intercostal bundle and distinguish its components.

concepts.subject: anatomy
concepts.title: Diaphragm: attachments, openings and breathing movement
concepts.summary: The diaphragm is a musculotendinous partition whose peripheral fibers converge on a central tendon. Contraction lowers its domes and increases thoracic height, while several major structures cross through or behind its attachments at distinct levels.
keyPoints: Peripheral attachments include xiphoid, costal margin, ribs 11–12 and posterior abdominal-wall/lumbar attachments. The central tendon is related to the attached pericardium.
Contraction flattens the domes and increases vertical thoracic dimension; relaxation allows elevation. This complements the AP/transverse expansion produced by rib movements.
Phrenic nerves derive from C3–C5 and supply the diaphragm from its abdominal surface. The lecture’s phrenic diagram explicitly supports the nerve course and motor supply.
The IVC passes through central tendon at approximately T8. The esophagus and vagal trunks cross muscular diaphragm near T10.
Aorta passes behind the posterior diaphragm at approximately T12 with the thoracic duct. Azygos/hemiazygos passage can vary between the aortic-hiatus and crural routes.
Sympathetic trunks pass posterior to peripheral attachments; thoracic splanchnic nerves penetrate the crura. These routes are different from the vagal esophageal route.

Arterial supply comes from above and below: pericardiacophrenic/musculophrenic branches of internal thoracic, superior phrenic branches of thoracic aorta, and larger inferior phrenic arteries from below.
Veins generally accompany the arteries and connect to brachiocephalic, azygos and abdominal venous systems. The broad supply pattern is more useful here than treating one artery as exclusive.
Openings and detailed attachment/supply notes are book-supported extensions; the slide emphasis visible in this set is chiefly the phrenic nerve and diaphragmatic landmark.
examTraps: The aorta passes behind the diaphragm, not through the central tendon.
Vagus accompanies esophagus; phrenic is the diaphragm’s motor nerve.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Match each major aperture to its contents and approximate level.
retrievalPrompts.answer: T8 central tendon: IVC; T10 muscular opening: esophagus and vagal trunks; T12 posterior/aortic route: aorta and thoracic duct.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does diaphragmatic contraction enlarge the thorax?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Peripheral muscle fibers contract toward the tendon, flattening/depressing the domes and increasing vertical thoracic dimension.

concepts.subject: histology
concepts.title: Conducting versus respiratory regions
concepts.summary: The airway changes function when alveoli first interrupt its wall, not simply when its diameter becomes small. Conducting structures condition and transport air; the respiratory region combines air passage with an alveolar gas-exchange surface.
keyPoints: The conducting sequence is nasal cavities, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and terminal bronchioles.
Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli constitute the respiratory region. Alveoli open directly from respiratory bronchiolar walls.
A terminal bronchiole may be surrounded by alveoli in a section without having alveoli opening into its own wall; surrounding lung tissue alone does not make it a respiratory bronchiole.
Cartilage, connective-tissue fibers and smooth muscle support conducting passages in different proportions; the most distal passages do not retain every support component.
Use a sequence of observations: cartilage/glands, epithelial height and cilia, continuity of the wall, then the distribution of alveolar openings.
examTraps: A small airway is not automatically a gas-exchange airway.
Alveoli beside an airway are not equivalent to alveoli opening from its wall.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What finding marks the first respiratory airway?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Alveoli opening directly from an otherwise bronchiolar wall identify a respiratory bronchiole.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace the distal sequence from the last conducting airway.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Terminal bronchiole → respiratory bronchiole → alveolar duct → alveolar sacs and alveoli.
