concepts.subject: physiology
concepts.title: Stretch, irritant, and juxtacapillary respiratory signals
concepts.summary: Pulmonary sensory receptors report different disturbances: excessive inflation, airway irritation, or interstitial/capillary congestion. Their anatomical location and stimulus explain why they should not be confused with arterial blood-gas chemoreceptors.
keyPoints: Bronchial and bronchiolar stretch receptors send vagal signals that terminate the inspiratory ramp during marked inflation: the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex.
In adults, the chapter presents the inflation reflex chiefly as protection against excessive inflation, not as the dominant timer of every normal quiet breath.

Airway irritant receptors respond to inhaled chemicals, inflammatory mediators, pathogens, mucus accumulation, and particulate stimulation. Responses include cough and, in some settings, bronchoconstriction.
The chapter names G-protein-coupled receptors and transient receptor potential channels as contributors to sensory transduction, without making one channel the sole detector of all irritants.
J receptors are sensory endings near pulmonary capillaries in alveolar walls. Capillary engorgement and interstitial edema are important stimuli.

J-receptor activation may contribute to dyspnea and increased respiratory rate; the text explicitly notes uncertainty about the full functional role, so this is taught as a plausible contribution rather than an exclusive cause.
Distinguish a mechanical inflation signal, an airway nociceptive/irritant signal, and an arterial PO2 signal from peripheral chemoreceptors.
examTraps: An edema-related J-receptor signal is not the same as a lung overinflation stretch signal.
Vagal pulmonary afferents do not all sense the same variable.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Match stretch, irritant, and J receptors to a typical stimulus.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Stretch receptors: marked lung inflation; irritant receptors: airway chemicals or particles; J receptors: capillary engorgement or pulmonary interstitial edema.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the main adult role assigned to the Hering-Breuer reflex?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Protection against excessive lung inflation by terminating inspiration, rather than routine control of every quiet breath.

concepts.subject: physiology
concepts.title: Anticipatory exercise ventilation and chemical fine-tuning
concepts.summary: Ventilation rises so quickly at exercise onset that a large prior arterial gas disturbance cannot explain all of the response. Neural commands accompanying movement provide anticipatory drive, while chemical feedback adjusts the match between ventilation and metabolism.
keyPoints: The chapter describes an immediate increase in ventilation accompanying initiation of muscle activity, before arterial PCO2, PO2, or pH changes enough to account for it.
A proposed major source is collateral neural signaling to brainstem respiratory centers while motor commands go to exercising muscles.

During steady exercise in healthy trained subjects, ventilation can rise approximately with metabolism, keeping arterial gases relatively close to resting levels; a large sustained CO2 rise is not required.
If anticipatory drive is too weak or too strong, chemical feedback adjusts ventilation. The feedback controller is still active during exercise rather than being disconnected.
Ventilation may initially lead metabolic CO2 delivery and briefly lower arterial PCO2; the time course helps distinguish anticipation from a response caused by prior hypercapnia.

The text describes evidence that part of this matching may be learned and involve cerebral cortex. This is a contribution to integrated control, not a claim that all exercise ventilation is consciously learned.
examTraps: An immediate response need not be triggered by a preceding rise in arterial CO2.
Near-normal exercise arterial gases can indicate successful control rather than absence of a greatly increased metabolic load.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What observation argues for anticipatory neural drive at exercise onset?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Ventilation increases before arterial gases have changed enough to explain the response.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What role remains for chemical feedback during exercise?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It corrects mismatch between neural drive and metabolic CO2/O2 exchange, helping maintain arterial gases.

concepts.subject: physiology
concepts.title: Cheyne-Stokes breathing: delay and excessive feedback gain
concepts.summary: Respiratory feedback can oscillate when a correction continues too long before updated gas information arrives or when the response to a small error is excessive. Cheyne-Stokes breathing is the waxing-and-waning pattern described by the chapter, with phases of deeper breathing and reduced breathing or apnea.
keyPoints: Overventilation lowers lung-blood CO2, but the altered blood must reach the brain before it inhibits respiratory drive. A delay allows the original correction to overshoot.
After drive falls, CO2 rises again, yet this change is also delivered with delay. Alternating overcorrection can sustain a repeating pattern.
Slow circulation in severe cardiac failure lengthens the lung-to-brain transport delay and can promote oscillation even without a primary increase in neural sensitivity.
A second mechanism is increased feedback gain: a small gas change produces an excessively large ventilatory response, for example with disordered respiratory-center function.
Normal storage and buffering of gases damp these oscillations. The presence of physiological delay alone does not mean every healthy person has Cheyne-Stokes breathing.
The respiratory center responds to its local arriving gas signal, which lags lung blood; Figure 42.12 illustrates this phase difference.
examTraps: Long delay and increased gain are two distinct mechanisms; one need not imply the other.
Lung-blood CO2 can change before the respiratory center receives the same change.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Explain the role of slow circulation in periodic breathing.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Delayed delivery of changed gases permits ventilatory corrections to overshoot before feedback arrives, producing alternating excess and deficient ventilation.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How can periodic breathing occur without an unusually long transport delay?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Excessive feedback gain can make the response to a small gas disturbance so large that the system oscillates.

concepts.subject: physiology
concepts.title: Obstructive, central, and mixed sleep apnea mechanisms
concepts.summary: Apnea during sleep can arise because an airway closes or because neural drive to ventilatory muscles transiently ceases. The resulting gas disturbances and repeated arousal fragment sleep, while mixed cases combine both mechanisms.
keyPoints: In obstructive apnea, relaxation of pharyngeal muscles permits a susceptible upper airway to narrow or close. Predisposing features described include narrowed passages, enlarged tonsils, large tongue, or excess surrounding soft tissue.
Airflow obstruction produces falling oxygen and rising carbon dioxide, stimulating attempts to breathe and episodes of arousal, snorting, or gasping.
Repeated events fragment sleep and can cause daytime drowsiness. The text also associates this pattern with increased sympathetic activity and cardiovascular consequences.
In central apnea, drive from the central nervous system to ventilatory muscles transiently ceases; a physical upper-airway obstruction is not required.
Central instability can occur with brain or neuromuscular disorders and may be worsened by drugs that depress respiratory responsiveness.
Mixed apnea combines obstructive and central mechanisms. The chapter's exact prevalence percentages and treatment selections are not used as definitive contemporary clinical guidance.
examTraps: Obstructive and central apnea are not differentiated simply by the word 'sleep'; the primary failed component differs.
Gas changes and sleep fragmentation can follow either mechanism.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What fails first in obstructive versus central apnea?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Obstructive apnea involves closure of the airflow passage; central apnea involves transient loss of neural ventilatory drive.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why can repeated apneas cause daytime sleepiness?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Repeated gas disturbances and arousals fragment restorative sleep.

concepts.subject: physiology
concepts.title: Voluntary breathing and pathological depression of drive
concepts.summary: Conscious breathing commands can temporarily alter ventilation enough to disturb blood gases, but this does not remove underlying metabolic requirements. Drugs or acute brain injury can instead suppress automatic respiratory drive and produce inadequate ventilation.
keyPoints: Voluntary hyperventilation can remove CO2 faster than metabolism supplies it; voluntary hypoventilation does the reverse. The effects concern effective alveolar ventilation, not respiratory rate alone.
At unchanged CO2 production, increased effective ventilation lowers PCO2 and tends to raise pH; reduced ventilation raises PCO2 and tends to lower pH.
Breath-holding eventually conflicts with gas-exchange needs. The chapter's extreme-record examples are not training targets, safety limits, or methods to reproduce.
Opioids and some anesthetic/sedative agents can depress respiratory-center activity and responsiveness to chemical stimuli. Severe depression can cause hypoventilation or respiratory arrest.
Acute brain edema can compromise cerebral perfusion and depress or inactivate respiratory control. This is a central cause, distinct from an isolated conducting-airway blockage.
These notes identify mechanisms only. The chapter's drug comparisons, hypertonic-fluid examples, and treatment recommendations are not converted into prescribing or resuscitation instructions.
examTraps: A voluntary command can change ventilation despite chemical feedback; it cannot abolish the body's continuing gas-exchange requirements.
Central depression can cause respiratory failure even when the airway is initially patent.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: At fixed metabolism, what happens to CO2 and pH during increased effective ventilation?
retrievalPrompts.answer: PCO2 falls as CO2 is removed faster, and pH tends to rise.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How can an opioid cause hypoventilation without narrowing the bronchi?
retrievalPrompts.answer: By depressing respiratory neural drive and its response to chemical stimulation.
